questions.question: What is the difference between a CSS transition and a CSS animation?
questions.title: CSS transitions versus animations
questions.direct_answer: A transition interpolates between an element's old and new property values after a state change. A CSS animation runs named @keyframes when animation properties apply, so it can have several stages, repeat, alternate, and start without a separate hover or class change.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner chooses motion tools by trigger and timeline complexity.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying transitions have two keyframes while missing that they require a property-value change.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the trigger, number of stages, and why simple state feedback should stay simple.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Transitions respond to a change between old and new property values.
Animations use named @keyframes and can define intermediate stages.
Animations can repeat or alternate without another state change.
Both interpolate only properties whose animation type allows it.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A CSS transition smooths a property when its computed value changes. I put the transition on the element, then a hover, focus, class, or media-query rule supplies the new value. The browser interpolates from the before-change value to the after-change value.

A CSS animation is an explicit timeline. `@keyframes` can describe a start, an end, and any intermediate stages, while animation properties control duration, delay, repetition, direction, and fill behaviour. The animation begins when its name applies, so it does not require a separate property change in the same way.

For example, a button color change on hover is naturally a transition because there are two UI states. A three-stage loading indicator that pulses continuously is naturally an animation because it has its own repeating timeline.

Neither tool makes every property smoothly interpolable, and motion should communicate change rather than delay the user. Interactive states must also work for keyboard focus, not only hover, and non-essential motion should respect the user's reduced-motion preference.

I choose a transition for a small state-to-state response and keyframes when the design truly needs an authored sequence or repetition. That keeps the stylesheet easier to read and gives the motion a clear reason to exist.

sections.title: State change or authored timeline
sections.content: A transition sits between two computed states and needs the second state to appear. An animation contributes animated values according to its keyframes while its animation name is active. Trigger and timeline—not visual complexity alone—separate the tools.

sections.title: The cascade still supplies the underlying values
sections.content: During a transition, the browser adds a current interpolated value to the cascade until the transition ends. An animation similarly supplies values from its current keyframe position. Removing the animation exposes the underlying author style again; using animation-fill-mode can extend a keyframe effect outside its active interval, but it does not rewrite the base declaration. Defining a stable base state prevents a flash or jump when the effect is unavailable.

sections.title: Choose by motion model
sections.content:
| Need | Transition | Animation |
|---|---|---|
| React to hover/class change | Natural fit | Possible |
| Three or more authored stages | Limited | Natural fit |
| Repeat independently | No | Yes |
| Keep final base state explicit | Yes | Yes |

sections.title: Use each tool for its natural job

questions.question: Which CSS properties should you animate for smooth performance?
questions.title: Smooth CSS animation with transform and opacity
questions.direct_answer: Prefer transform and opacity for frequent visual motion because browsers can often composite them without recalculating document layout or repainting surrounding content. Measure the real page, because compositing and layer promotion are optimizations rather than guarantees.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner connects property changes to style, layout, paint, and compositing work.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating 'GPU accelerated' as a guarantee or adding will-change to every element.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why layout-changing properties cost more and show how to measure frames.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: transform changes visual geometry without moving neighbouring layout boxes.
opacity changes transparency and is commonly composited.
width, height, top, and left may trigger layout and paint work.
Use performance tools to confirm the actual bottleneck.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Smooth animation depends on how much rendering work each frame causes. Properties such as width or left can require layout, and layout changes may force parts of the page to paint again. That becomes expensive when many elements or a large subtree are involved.

`transform` changes the rendered position, scale, or rotation without changing the element's normal-flow layout box. `opacity` changes transparency. Browsers can often handle these effects during compositing, which avoids repeated layout and may avoid paint work for the moving content.

For example, I would slide a notification with `transform: translateY()` rather than animating `top`. Sibling content keeps its original layout position, and the browser only needs to update the notification's visual transform through the frames.

This is a preference, not a promise that every transformed element gets a GPU layer. Large layers consume memory, filters and shadows may still be costly, and `will-change` used everywhere can make performance worse. I add it only for a measured, imminent change and remove it when it is no longer needed.

I check the browser's Performance panel for long frames, layout, and paint activity, and test on a representative mobile device. The right property choice is the starting point; measurement confirms whether the animation actually meets the frame budget.

sections.title: Every frame passes through a rendering pipeline
sections.content: A visual change may require style calculation, layout, paint, and compositing. Skipping earlier work usually leaves less work per frame. transform and opacity are commonly chosen because they can preserve layout and often let the compositor update an existing painted layer.

sections.title: Why translating is not the same as changing top
sections.content: Changing `top` on a positioned element changes a layout input. The browser may need to recalculate geometry before it knows what to paint. A transform operates on the element's rendered result, so its original box still occupies the same normal-flow position. That distinction also means transforms do not make other content reflow out of the way; if layout really must change, animate sparingly or use a discrete state change instead of disguising it.

sections.title: Typical work triggered per frame
sections.content:
left / width change → style → layout → paint → composite
transform / opacity → style → often composite only
                         ↑ verify the actual path in Performance tools

sections.title: Move a notice without changing layout geometry

questions.question: How do @keyframes and animation properties control an animation's lifecycle?
questions.title: The CSS animation lifecycle
questions.direct_answer: @keyframes defines property values along a timeline, while animation-duration, delay, timing-function, iteration-count, direction, and fill-mode determine how that timeline plays. The base element style still matters before, after, or whenever the animation does not run.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner understands animation phases rather than memorizing the animation shorthand.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using forwards as a substitute for a correct persistent state or forgetting that delay is outside the active duration.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain delay, active iterations, direction, and fill as separate controls.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: @keyframes maps timeline positions to CSS property values.
Duration and iteration count determine active running time.
Direction changes how alternating iterations traverse the keyframes.
Fill mode controls whether keyframe effects apply before or after the active phase.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`@keyframes` names a sequence of property values at offsets from 0% to 100%. Applying that name creates an animation whose duration maps wall-clock time onto those offsets. A timing function changes the rate of progress between keyframes; it does not add another keyframe.

The delay creates time before the active phase, and iteration-count says how many times the timeline runs. Direction can play the sequence normally, in reverse, or alternate direction on successive iterations. Fill mode decides whether the first or final keyframe effect is visible outside the active phase.

For example, a success check can draw once over 500 milliseconds and finish in its completed visual state. The application's persistent success class should still define the stable result, rather than relying only on `forwards`, because disabling or removing the animation must not remove meaning.

Intermediate keyframes can omit a property; the browser then uses the relevant underlying or interpolated values according to the animation model. Multiple animations can run together, so the shorthand should keep matching comma-separated values aligned by position.

I treat keyframes as a temporary presentation over a sound base state. That makes the interface understandable when animation is unsupported, reduced, interrupted, or restarted, and it keeps application state separate from a decorative timeline.

sections.title: Three phases around one active timeline
sections.content: An animation has a before phase, an active phase, and an after phase. Delay, duration, and iteration count locate those phases in time. Direction and timing functions control travel during the active phase, while fill mode controls whether keyframe effects extend outside it.

sections.title: Fill mode affects presentation, not application truth
sections.content: `animation-fill-mode: forwards` retains the values produced by the animation's ending position after the active interval. It does not modify the element's authored base declarations or record business state. If a panel is truly open or a task truly complete, a class, attribute, or DOM state should express that fact. Keyframes may decorate the change, and the base state should remain correct when motion is removed.

sections.title: One animation across time
sections.content:
before phase     active phase: iteration 1 | iteration 2     after phase
<--- delay ---><----------- duration × count ------------------->
    backwards?          direction + timing function              forwards?

sections.title: Animate once over an explicit base state

questions.question: How should a site respect prefers-reduced-motion?
questions.title: Designing for reduced motion
questions.direct_answer: Use the prefers-reduced-motion media query to suppress or replace non-essential movement when the user requests less motion. Preserve the same information and task completion with a static state, a short fade, or no effect rather than hiding functionality.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner treats reduced motion as a design requirement, not a blanket duration trick.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Setting every duration to nearly zero while continuous transforms, parallax, or autoplay still exist.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish essential state feedback from decorative spatial movement.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: prefers-reduced-motion: reduce reflects a user or system preference.
Remove or replace non-essential movement, especially large spatial motion.
Keep information and controls available in the reduced version.
Test with the operating system preference enabled.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`prefers-reduced-motion` lets CSS respond when a user has asked the operating system or browser for less non-essential movement. The goal is to prevent motion that can distract or trigger discomfort, not to remove the information that the interface communicates.

I begin with a complete static state, then add decorative movement inside `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)`. This opt-in pattern means the stable experience remains the default whenever the preference or animation support is uncertain.

For example, a route change might normally slide the new page across the viewport. In reduced mode it can appear immediately or use a gentle opacity change. The heading, focus movement, loading status, and completion message must remain identical in meaning.

Some movement can be essential to understanding a demonstration, but it still needs controls or an equivalent explanation. Simply changing a five-second animation to one millisecond can also cause flashing or make a sequence impossible to follow, so each effect needs a deliberate alternative.

I enable reduced motion at the system level and exercise every interactive effect, including scroll-linked motion, parallax, auto-playing decoration, and hover transitions. A compliant query in one stylesheet is not enough unless the whole task works comfortably in that mode.

sections.title: Preserve meaning while reducing movement
sections.content: Reduced motion is an alternate presentation of the same state change. The user should still know what opened, saved, failed, or completed. Remove decorative travel first; retain necessary feedback through text, position, color with sufficient contrast, or restrained non-spatial changes.

sections.title: Why opt-in motion is resilient
sections.content: When the static layout is the base, components do not depend on an animation finishing before they become usable. A no-preference query then adds enhancement for users who have not requested reduction. This also handles interrupted animations more safely. For interaction-triggered motion, WAI's technique recommends checking each effect with the reduction preference enabled and ensuring that essential animation is either necessary or suppressed.

sections.title: One event, equivalent outcomes
sections.content:
panel opens
├─ no-preference → panel slides in → focus enters heading
└─ reduce        → panel appears   → focus enters heading
                   same content, control, and final state

sections.title: Make motion an optional enhancement
